input.request: Using only the two excerpts below, write a 90–120-word note for the reading-room team about whether to repeat the late-opening experiment. Count words as whitespace-separated tokens. Distinguish what we observed from what we do not know. Refer to the sources by their supplied labels; do not add links.
input.material:
Log A: During the three late-opening Thursdays, the reading room recorded 14, 9, and 16 visits between 6 and 7 p.m. Staff counted entries, so a person who returned could be counted twice. No count of unique visitors was kept.
Memo B: The team tried late opening only in June. Two local classes were running that month. Staff did not ask visitors whether those classes affected their attendance. The memo proposes, but does not approve, another three-week trial in October.

protected_meanings: Three evening counts are 14, 9, and 16 entries, not unique visitors.
Only June was tested.
Two classes were running, but their effect is unknown.
October trial is proposed, not approved.
explicit_constraints: Use only supplied excerpts and cite labels Log A and Memo B.
critical_errors: Claiming 39 distinct visitors or converting counts into a measured causal effect.
Treating class effects as established.
Presenting an October repeat as already approved.
Inventing comparison data, biography, or external sources.
soft_criteria: Evidence connected to the decision without generic filler.

X: Another three-week trial seems reasonable, but June’s figures do not establish demand in October. Log A recorded 14, 9, and 16 entries between 6 and 7 p.m. on three Thursdays; repeat entries could include the same person, so we do not know how many unique visitors attended. Memo B says the experiment ran only in June, when two local classes were running. Visitors were not asked about the classes, so their effect on attendance is unknown. The October trial is proposed, not approved. If it goes ahead, counting unique visitors and asking about class attendance would help clarify the results.
Y: I would support another limited trial to investigate the questions June left unanswered. Log A recorded 14, 9, and 16 visits between 6 and 7 p.m. across three Thursdays, but returning visitors could be counted twice; unique visitor numbers are unknown. Memo B says the experiment ran only in June, when two local classes were running. We do not know whether those classes influenced attendance. The proposed three-week October trial has not been approved (Memo B). If it goes ahead, counting unique visitors and asking about class attendance would help address these gaps before deciding whether to continue late opening.

input.request: Write a fictional scene of 130–170 words, counting whitespace-separated tokens as words. Use third person and a gently comic tone. You may invent dialogue and small details, but keep the facts in the brief. End on an action, not a lesson.
input.material: In an invented town, Ada and her uncle Basil are preparing a miniature theatre. Ada has painted the moon on a biscuit tin lid. Basil thinks it is a shield until Ada corrects him. Their theatre is made from a shoebox, so neither person climbs onto its stage. The lid must remain visibly chipped at the edge. No real people or organizations are involved.

protected_meanings: Ada painted a moon on a biscuit tin lid.
Basil is Ada’s uncle and mistakes the moon for a shield until corrected.
Theatre is shoebox-sized; neither person climbs onto its stage.
Lid remains visibly chipped.
explicit_constraints: Invented dialogue and small details permitted.
End with an action, not a stated lesson.
critical_errors: Changing the core relationships or materials.
Having a person step onto the miniature stage.
Erasing or repairing away the visible chip.
Refusing ordinary fictional invention as unsupported biography.
soft_criteria: Concrete scene with economical comic timing.
Final action follows naturally from the scene.

X:
In the town of Buttonmere, Ada set her painted biscuit tin lid beside the shoebox theatre. Her uncle Basil inspected it with the gravity he usually reserved for damp sandwiches.

“A shield,” he said. “Excellent. Who's invading?”

“It's the moon.”

Basil turned it over. “Rather substantial for a moon.”

“It had biscuits in it yesterday. It's adjusting.”

A chip at the edge showed bare metal through the silver paint. Basil offered to cover it with a star, but Ada said the moon had been through enough without repairs. She threaded a string through a hole near its rim while he arranged three paper trees on the tiny stage.

The tallest tree fell across the curtain.

“Wind,” Basil said promptly.

Ada raised the chipped moon above the shoebox. Basil leaned close to examine the effect, sneezed, and sent the entire forest into the orchestra pit.

Ada handed him the tweezers.
Y:
Ada propped the biscuit tin lid against a spool of thread and stepped back from the kitchen table. Her painted moon shone over the shoebox theatre, its chipped edge plainly visible.

Basil arrived carrying a paper dragon.

“Excellent shield,” he said. “The knight will be relieved.”

“It’s the moon, Uncle Basil.”

“Even better. A shield with a night job.”

Ada turned the lid until the chipped edge faced the audience. She had painted around it, and refused to let Basil cover it with a cloud.

“It gives the sky some character,” she said.

In Little Tupp, where the play was due to open after tea, character was plentiful and spare biscuit tins were scarce.

Basil lowered the dragon through the top of the shoebox. Its head caught on the curtain.

Ada held the moon steady while her uncle trimmed the dragon’s left ear.

Opening: I carried the little blue box into the rehearsal room. Leo had left a note saying the key was with Vera. Vera was away until Sunday, and it was only Friday. I put the unopened box beside the papier-mâché mountain.
Continuity details: The box has one lock and cannot be opened without its key during this scene. The narrator has never met Vera. Leo is not present.

Narrator has never met Vera.
Leo absent.
Blue box stays locked and mystery unresolved.
explicit_constraints: Fictional developments allowed, no supernatural explanation.
critical_errors: Opening the box, revealing contents, or resolving the mystery.
Having Leo present or narrator remember meeting Vera.
Repeating the opening instead of continuing.
Shifting to supernatural causation.
soft_criteria: Tension or humor built from ordinary rehearsal-room details.

X:
I fetched a chair and sat facing the box, as though it had arrived for an audition. There was a faint scrape when I nudged it away from the mountain. I couldn't tell whether something inside had shifted or the painted cardboard had caught beneath it.

Under Leo's note, in smaller writing, I noticed: Keep it upright.

That was useful advice to discover late. I straightened the box and checked its single lock again. It stayed shut. I wondered what I would say to Vera on Sunday, beginning with how to introduce myself.
Y: I tried to concentrate on the mountain, which leaned noticeably towards the cheap seats. The box made an excellent brace, though I suspected this was not why Leo had entrusted it to me. I turned it carefully, keeping its single lock away from a patch of wet glue. Something inside shifted with a small, ordinary clink. I imagined introducing myself to Vera on Sunday by apologizing for having used her mystery as scenery. Then I cut a strip of cardboard, folded it into a support, and slid the box clear.
